concept.name: Dollar-cost averaging
concept.definition: An accumulation strategy that invests a fixed dollar amount into an asset at regular intervals regardless of price, so that more units are bought when prices are low and fewer when prices are high. It replaces market-timing decisions with a mechanical purchase schedule.
concept.intuition: A fixed $500 buys twice as many shares at $10 as at $20, so the average cost per share ends up below the average price over the period - the schedule does the buying-low work automatically.
concept.mechanics: Divide the planned investment into equal tranches and deploy them on a fixed calendar (weekly, monthly, quarterly). Regulator education stresses that DCA changes when and how money is invested; it does not prevent losses or guarantee returns.
concept.formula: Average cost per share = n x A / sum(A / P_i) = n / sum(1 / P_i), the harmonic mean of purchase prices P_i for fixed amount A per period.
concept.failure_modes: In a steadily rising market DCA underperforms investing the lump sum up front because cash sits idle, and in a secular decline it systematically buys into losses; frequent small purchases can also carry proportionally high fees.
concept.misconceptions: That DCA is a timing strategy that beats the market or removes risk; its benefit is behavioral discipline and timing-risk smoothing, and it still loses money in sustained downturns.
concept.example: Investing $250 weekly into an ETF priced at $99, $96, $97, and $100 produces an average share cost of about $98.00, versus $99.00 for a week-one lump-sum purchase (CIRO illustration).

citations.source: CIRO (Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization), 'Dollar Cost Averaging'
citations.section: What is Dollar Cost Averaging; How Does Dollar Cost Averaging Work
